rule_name: Banned Constructions, Assert Nothing, Show the Substance
quote: it looks really good
why: the line's entire content is a verdict on quality with no supporting evidence, the exact banned pattern of rule 1
suggestion: "The scroll's dead straight," she says, turning it under the light.

rule_name: Hedge Where the Character Could Not Know, Cut Filler Everywhere Else
quote: really good
why: "really" is on the explicit filler cut list and softens a claim without adding information
suggestion: cut it: "it looks good."

rule_name: STYLE_RULES 8: Automatic-fail narrator constructions -- Superlatives in narration
quote: Nobody else in the year does that
why: an absolute superlative asserted flatly by the narrator; the banned-list fix says cut these, they are fine only in dialogue
suggestion: cut it, or give it to a character: "Nobody else does that," Odile says, and nobody corrects her.

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: Chloe finds she is looking at the top of Ruth's head
why: "finds" routes the observation through a perception verb instead of rendering the fact directly
suggestion: She is looking at the top of Ruth's head.

quote: "I haven't said anything to you at all." smirking.
why: a bare participle stands as its own sentence, not attached to any speech tag -- this is rule 35's own named example almost verbatim
suggestion: "I haven't said anything to you at all," she says, smirking.

rule_name: STYLE_RULES 8: Automatic-fail narrator constructions -- Superlatives in narration
quote: the correction is the only sentence he says to her before Christmas
why: narrator superlative ("the only") stated as flat fact; the table says cut these on sight in narration
suggestion: cut the clause, or render the silence: he doesn't speak to her again before Christmas.

rule_name: STYLE_RULES 8: Automatic-fail narrator constructions -- Interiority of non-POV characters
quote: he has stopped caring about bread
why: states Kavi's internal mental state as narrated fact, but Chloe is the POV character and Kavi is not
suggestion: he has gone quiet on the bread argument and is writing numbers on the back of his hand

quote: at 4
why: numeral "4" breaks house style against "four in the morning" spelled out twice in the same sentence -- this is rule 35's own numeral example, down to the exact phrase "at 4"
suggestion: she has done a watch at four in the morning

quote: "Nobody said anything about tonight.", Ruth arrives
why: a stray comma follows the closing quotation mark before an action beat that is not a speech tag
suggestion: "Nobody said anything about tonight." Ruth arrives with her hair everywhere.

quote: thirty seconds."It's AES-256,"
why: missing space between the end of the narrative sentence and the opening quotation mark
suggestion: thirty seconds. "It's AES-256,"

quote: wiping his face, “Why wouldn’t they change it?”
why: a comma splices a completed tag-plus-action beat directly into a new quoted sentence in place of a period
suggestion: Sam says, wiping his face. "Why wouldn't they change it?"

quote: copy," Kavi says.
why: "Kavi says" is used as the frame verb three times in a twelve-line span (165, 169, 177), the exact repeated-tag failure the checklist flags
suggestion: drop the tag on this instance since only Kavi is speaking in the exchange, or vary it: Kavi keeps going.

quote: "Why would they take the stairs."
why: an interrogative sentence is closed with a period instead of a question mark, inconsistent with every other question in the chapter
suggestion: "Why would they take the stairs?"

quote: Ruth looks at her, "I’m shorter," Ruth says.
why: a comma splices an action beat directly into a new quoted sentence in place of a period, matching rule 35's own cut example
suggestion: Ruth looks at her. "I'm shorter," she says.

quote: I look smaller, It's psychology
why: stray capitalization follows a comma mid-sentence, the exact defect named in rule 35
suggestion: I look smaller, it's psychology

rule_name: STYLE_RULES 8: Automatic-fail narrator constructions -- Interiority of non-POV characters
quote: Ruth thinks about it for about as long as it takes to breathe out
why: states Ruth's internal cognitive process as narrated fact; Chloe is the POV character and Ruth is not, matching the banned example "Sam thinks about it longer than he wants to" almost exactly
suggestion: Ruth is quiet for as long as it takes to breathe out.

quote: Fine, Fast ones
why: stray capitalization follows a comma mid-sentence
suggestion: Fine, fast ones

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: She knows the face
why: "knows" is one of the filter verbs rule 24 names explicitly and puts a pane of glass between the reader and the expression itself
suggestion: She has the face ready, confused and half asleep.

quote: "Hi. Who are you?", tilting her head like a lost puppy.
why: a dangling participle follows a comma after the closing quotation mark, not attached to any subject or tag
suggestion: "Hi. Who are you?" she says, tilting her head like a lost puppy.

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: just like she knew he wouldn't
why: "knew" is a filter verb that reports Chloe's certainty instead of rendering the physical fact that grounds it
suggestion: just like she'd guessed from the way he moved

quote: Then it's very fast and very quiet.
why: the present-tense equivalent of "it was" plus adjectives, a weak-verb construction that tells the reader how to feel instead of creating the feeling
suggestion: Then it's over in nine seconds, and nobody shouts.

rule_name: Sentence Rhythm, Break the Subject-Verb-Object Drumbeat
quote: Kavi takes the two at the back because he's closest to them. Ruth takes the third. Sam takes the one with his hand on Chloe's face
why: three consecutive sentences share the identical name-verb-object shape, producing the flat witness-statement rhythm rule 11 bans
suggestion: Kavi, closest, takes the two at the back; Ruth takes the third, and Sam goes for the one with his hand on Chloe's face.

rule_name: Let Register Escalate With the Moment, Earn Flatness by Contrast
quote: Kavi takes the two at the back because he's closest to them. Ruth takes the third. Sam takes the one with his hand on Chloe's face
why: the chapter's most violent moment is rendered in the same flat declarative rhythm used for the forge and dinner scenes, so the flatness never registers as a choice
suggestion: let one sentence run longer and more physical before the flat count-off, so the shortness afterward lands by contrast

quote: "Both were in eventually." Kavi says.
why: the quote is closed with a period and the tag follows as its own fragment instead of a comma joining one continuous sentence
suggestion: "Both were in eventually," Kavi says.

quote: we are losing marks" Ruth says.
why: missing comma before the closing quotation mark before the attribution tag
suggestion: we are losing marks," Ruth says.

quote: "That's the sensors."Kavi says.
why: no space before the tag and a period instead of a comma joining the quote to the attribution
suggestion: "That's the sensors," Kavi says.

quote: Four's fine, Four's happened
why: stray capitalization follows a comma mid-sentence
suggestion: Four's fine, four's happened

quote: as long as They tell you
why: a second stray capital in the same line, mid-sentence with no proper noun to justify it
suggestion: as long as they tell you

quote: "Escalation. We've been good." Kavi says.
why: the quote is closed with a period and the tag follows as a disconnected fragment instead of a comma
suggestion: "Escalation. We've been good," Kavi says.

rule_name: Repetition as Emphasis, Say It Once and Let Placement Do the Work
quote: she says again
why: the narration flags its own repetition of "four in the morning," already said twice by Ruth two lines earlier, with no new information added
suggestion: cut the repeated line and let "and she puts her head back against the wall" stand alone

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: confused for a while
why: "for a while" is named directly as a universal duration marker regardless of what is being timed
suggestion: confused for a beat

quote: and then he seems to realize that he's tied, and then he sees who tied him
why: two clauses of unequal weight are coordinated with repeated "and then" instead of subordinated, flattening the escalation
suggestion: before he realizes he's tied, and sees who tied him

rule_name: Repetition as Emphasis, Say It Once and Let Placement Do the Work
quote: He doesn't say anything.
why: identical to the narration four lines earlier at line 287 with no new information, texture, or reaction added by the repeat
suggestion: He looks at the wall instead.

quote: writes something on her arm
why: "something" stands in for a concrete, nameable detail the scene already has available (a number, a word)
suggestion: writes a dash on her arm

quote: He doesn't answer, and his face does, and Kavi says "server room" and writes it down.
why: three clauses of unequal weight are coordinated flatly with repeated "and" instead of subordinated
suggestion: He doesn't answer, though his face does; Kavi says "server room" and writes it down.

quote: wakes up about a minute later and is younger and seems to be less good at keeping his face still
why: three separate observations are coordinated with repeated "and" instead of given a hierarchy
suggestion: wakes up about a minute later, younger, less good at keeping his face still

rule_name: Talking Heads, Anchor Dialogue in Physical Space
quote: "Four seconds of compute."
why: from line 303 to line 317 the interrogation runs roughly seven dialogue turns with no physical detail beyond bare tags, leaving the reader without bodies in the corridor
suggestion: drop in a physical beat, e.g. Kavi turns his wrist to check the time. "Four seconds of compute."

rule_name: Repetition as Emphasis, Say It Once and Let Placement Do the Work
quote: "Four seconds," Sam says.
why: Sam repeats Kavi's "four seconds of compute" from the line before verbatim with no new information, matching rule 4's own example pattern
suggestion: cut Sam's line, or make it react: "Four seconds," Sam says, like it offends him.

quote: nobody told us, There was nothing on the board
why: stray capitalization follows a comma mid-sentence
suggestion: nobody told us, there was nothing on the board

quote: “I was enjoying my sleep too” Ruth pipes up.
why: missing comma before the closing quotation mark before the attribution tag
suggestion: “I was enjoying my sleep too,” Ruth pipes up.

quote: What would you give us."
why: an interrogative sentence closed with a period instead of a question mark
suggestion: What would you give us?"

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a long moment
why: a generic duration marker standing in for a specific, rendered beat
suggestion: The man's jaw works once.

quote: walking back with his hands up, "That's a C right there."
why: a comma splices a completed tag-plus-action beat into a new quoted sentence in place of a period
suggestion: walking back with his hands up. "That's a C right there."

quote: something about it isn't sitting right
why: "something" is used as emotional shorthand for a specific unease the sentence never names
suggestion: the boots don't match the fence they came over, and she can't stop looking at them

rule_name: STYLE_RULES 11: Structure -- Mystery lives in characters' mouths, never in narration
quote: The bolt cutters are wrong. The boots are wrong. All of it is wrong in the same direction and she can't make the direction mean anything
why: the narrator builds and dwells on an unresolved suspicion directly in Chloe's narrated interiority instead of putting it in a character's mouth as the rule requires
suggestion: have Chloe say it aloud to someone, even dismissed: "The boots are wrong," she says. Nobody's listening.

quote: watching them."Who's monitoring?"
why: missing space and missing sentence break between the narrative clause and the opening quotation mark
suggestion: watching them. "Who's monitoring?"

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a second just watching them
why: "for a second" is named directly in rule 27 as a universal duration marker regardless of what is being timed
suggestion: watching them without moving

quote: which she is unbearable about
why: the sentence is complete before the comma; the trailing clause exists only to tell the reader how to take the fact, exactly what rule 5 cuts
suggestion: Ruth gets a B minus. She brings it up for a week.

rule_name: Dialogue Tag Clutter, Let Action Beats Carry Tone
quote: Chloe says, sitting against the wall with her arms around her knees.
why: the tag is loaded with a full participial description of posture instead of splitting the physical detail into its own sentence
suggestion: Chloe sits against the wall with her arms around her knees. "It's still going to be slow."

rule_name: Adjective-as-Adverb Dialogue Tags ("She Says It Tired")
quote: He looks at her confused.
why: an adjective is used where an adverb or physical detail belongs, labeling the expression instead of rendering it, the same shortcut rule 20 bans in tags
suggestion: He looks at her, brow creased.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: For a second the only thing moving
why: "for a second" is named directly in rule 27 as a universal duration marker regardless of what is being timed
suggestion: The only thing moving at that end of the table is the steam.

quote: which she never does
why: the sentence is complete before the comma; the trailing clause exists only to tell the reader the action is significant, exactly what the trailing-clause and superlative-in-narration rules cut
suggestion: Then she puts the spoon down on the cloth.

quote: you are 12 years old
why: numeral "12" breaks house style against "twelve" spelled out repeatedly elsewhere in the chapter (lines 49, 199, 325)
suggestion: you are twelve years old

quote: "Okay. I'll stay in my room." she sighs.
why: the quote is closed with a period and the tag follows lowercase as a fragment instead of a comma joining one continuous sentence

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: that's the end of it
why: "and that's the end of it" is named directly in rule 27 as a reflexive scene-closer that has stopped meaning anything
